sections.title: The Problem
points: Large photos, videos, and documents consume application bandwidth and memory. Transfers can exceed request deadlines and overload relational storage.
Separate permission checks and metadata from file transfer. Application servers manage access. Object storage receives and serves the bytes.

sections.title: The Solution
points: Store file bytes in object storage. Store metadata in a database.
Give the client temporary permission for a specific transfer. The client sends bytes directly to object storage.
Use a CDN for frequent downloads. Use multipart uploads for large files or unreliable connections.

sections.title: 1) Direct upload
points: The client requests permission to upload a file. The request includes its expected size, type, and owner.
The server validates the request. It creates pending metadata and signs the upload instructions with its local credentials.
The client uploads directly to object storage. The backend verifies the completed object before it makes the file available.
A signed URL permits a specific operation on a specific object. It does not give the client unrestricted storage credentials.

flows.title: Upload bytes directly to object storage
steps: The client requests upload permission through the API Gateway. It supplies the expected file metadata.
The server validates the user and transfer limits. It signs a URL for the intended object with its local credentials.
The server returns the signed URL to the client.
The client sends the file directly to object storage with the permitted upload request. Application servers do not forward the bytes.

sections.title: 2) Direct download
points: The service authenticates the caller. It checks file permissions before it issues a signed download URL.
The client downloads from object storage or a CDN. A CDN validates its own signed URL or cookie.
Set the URL lifetime and cache policy to match the content's sensitivity. Define how permission changes affect existing URLs.
A person with an issued URL can use it until it expires. An application permission change might not revoke it immediately.

flows.title: Download through the CDN
steps: The application checks access before it issues a signed CDN URL.
The client sends the download request to the CDN. The CDN validates the signed URL.
If the CDN has a permitted cached copy, it returns that copy.
On a cache miss, the CDN fetches the object from blob storage. It returns the bytes to the client.

sections.title: 3) Resumable uploads
points: Split the file into numbered parts. Keep the upload ID and the storage provider's confirmation for each part.
After an interruption, upload only missing or failed parts. Then ask object storage to assemble the file.
Limit parallel transfers and part size. These limits prevent excessive client memory use and network connections.
Expire abandoned upload sessions. Remove incomplete parts to limit storage costs.

flows.title: Retry only the unfinished parts
steps: The client uses the upload session and the provider's SDK to divide the file into numbered parts.
The client uploads parts directly to object storage. It keeps the provider's confirmations and the session identifier.
After an interruption, the client checks which parts already exist in that session.
The client uploads the missing parts. It then requests completion with the required part identifiers.
Object storage assembles the parts into one object. An incomplete multipart upload does not yet provide the completed file.

sections.title: 4) State synchronization
points: The database and object storage do not share one transaction. Track pending uploads separately from completed files.
Verify a client completion message with a storage API or a trusted storage event.
Storage events can repeat or arrive late. Make completion updates idempotent. Periodically check uploads that remain pending.
A multipart event can describe only the completed object. Use the provider's multipart APIs to verify individual parts.

flows.title: Confirm storage completion in the database
steps: The server creates pending metadata with the object key before it authorizes the upload.
The client uploads the file to blob storage. Multipart uploads must complete before the final object is available.
Blob storage emits an object completion event. The object key identifies the pending database record.
The backend verifies the completion evidence. It updates the matching record without creating a second result for a repeated event.
A periodic job checks records that remain pending. It compares their state with object storage and repairs missed updates.

sections.title: Cloud Provider Terminology
points: Providers use different names for signed URLs, multipart uploads, object versions, and completion checks.
Explain the required capability and its failure behavior. A product name alone does not explain the design.

sections.title: Common Deep Dives
points: If a transfer fails at 99%, resume from verified parts. Do not upload completed parts again.
Check quotas, maximum file size, permitted content types, and session lifetime before granting access. Quarantine uploads until required scans pass.
Store the owner, object key, size, checksum, version, and processing state in the database. Keep these records separate from file bytes.
An ETag is not always a hash of the complete file. Its meaning depends on the provider and upload mode.

sections.title: Metadata and Download Performance
points: Give each immutable object version a separate identity. This simplifies caching and prevents mixed content during replacement.
Use range requests to resume downloads. A CDN serves popular content near users. Media variants reduce unnecessary transfer size.
Run scans, thumbnail generation, and transcoding in background workers. Keep this work outside the metadata request.

sections.title: Conclusion
points: Direct signed transfers reduce application bandwidth use. The application still controls permissions, metadata, and completion checks.
A complete design includes multipart recovery, cleanup, access control, and periodic checks for inconsistent state.
